summary:
Walk through the badges once while remembering every number seen in a hash set. The first number
that's already in the set is a duplicate. That's O(n) time, against O(n²) for comparing all pairs
and O(n log n) for sorting.

question.md:
Return `true` if any number appears **at least twice** in the list, otherwise `false`.

- **Any repeat counts**, anywhere in the list, not just next to each other.
- **One badge** can't repeat: `[5]` is `false`.
- **Negative numbers** are allowed, so tricks that use the numbers as array indices don't work
  directly (values go from −10⁹ to 10⁹).
- **Size:** up to 10⁵ badges. Comparing every pair is ~5 × 10⁹ comparisons.
- You can **stop at the first repeat**: the answer is just yes or no.

think.md:
Take `[12, 5, 9, 2, 5, 8]`. Reading it left to right as a person would, you keep a mental list of
numbers you've passed: 12, 5, 9, 2… then another 5. "I've seen 5." Done.

That mental list is the whole algorithm. The question is only how quickly you can check "have I
seen this?":

- scanning everything before it costs O(n) per check, O(n²) in total;
- sorting first puts equal numbers next to each other, so a single neighbour check finds them;
- a hash set answers "seen it?" in O(1) on average.

think.caption: The repeat is at indices 1 and 4, three places apart.

approaches.title: Compare every pair

idea.md: Check every pair `i < j`. If any two are equal, return true. If no pair matches, return false.

build: Loop `i` over indices and `j` from `i + 1` to the end.

lines.text: Every pair of different positions, each pair once.
Two equal badges: that's a duplicate, and nothing else needs checking.
No pair matched, so every number is different.

steps.text: Badge 12 (index 0) against the 5 after it: no match.

walk.title: Compare every badge with every badge after it.

limits.md: The "have I seen this?" question is answered by re-reading the list. Sorting or a hash set answers it far faster.

approaches.title: Sort, then check neighbours

idea.md: After sorting, equal numbers are adjacent, so a duplicate exists exactly when some neighbouring pair is equal.

build: Sort a copy of the badges.
Return true if any `s[i] == s[i + 1]`, else false.

lines.text: Comparator for `qsort`, safe for values near ±10⁹ (no subtraction).
Sort a copy so equal numbers become neighbours, leaving the input untouched.
Only neighbours need comparing now: if a number repeats, one of its copies sits right next to another.
No equal neighbours means no repeats.

complexity.md: **Time O(n log n)** for the sort. **Space O(n)** for the copy (O(1) extra if sorting the input in place is allowed).

steps.text: 5 and 5 are neighbours and equal. Duplicate.

walk.title: Sort a copy; equal numbers end up side by side.

limits.md: Sorting orders every number, which is more than "is anything repeated?" needs. A hash set skips the ordering and can stop at the first repeat without reading the rest.

approaches.title: Hash set of numbers seen

idea.md: Walk left to right with a hash set. If the current badge is already in the set, return true; otherwise add it. If the walk ends, every badge was new.

build: For each badge: if it's in the set, return true; else add it.

lines.text: C has no hash set, so here's a minimal one: each slot holds a key and an in-use flag. `slotOf` scrambles a key into a starting slot by multiplying by a large odd constant and keeping the well-mixed high bits.
An empty set of numbers seen so far.

notes.c: A power-of-two table at least twice the number of badges, zeroed by `calloc` (every slot unused). `dup` lets the loop stop early and still free the table.

lines.text: Seen before? Then it's a duplicate.

notes.java: `add` returns false when the value was already present: one call both checks and inserts.
notes.cpp: `insert` returns a pair whose `.second` is false when the value was already present.
notes.c: Probe from the badge's slot, stepping forward past other keys. A used slot holding our key means seen; an empty slot means new.
Claim the empty slot the probe stopped at.

complexity.md: **Time O(n)** on average: one O(1) check and insert per badge, and it stops early at the first repeat. **Space O(n)** for the set.

steps.text: 5 is already in the set. Duplicate.

walk.title: Remember every badge seen so far in a hash set.

takeaways.md:
- "Have I seen this before?" is a hash-set question: O(1) per check.
- Sorting turns "equal somewhere" into "equal neighbours", a good fallback when extra memory is
  tight.
- Stop as soon as the answer is known; a yes/no question rarely needs the whole input.
